records.title: Show HN: Jurl – curl that reads the page for you
records.author: rayoplateado
records.storyText:
jurl is a CLI. Tell it what you want from a page and it picks exactly that out: the paragraphs that answer a question, the code, the links worth following, or a photo you describe. On Wikipedia's Cologne page it finds the cathedral among 73 images in 2.3 s; on the Jevons page, the two paragraphs out of ~240 that explain his paradox.

The link above lets you try it in the browser, no key needed. Or in your terminal, with your own TypeSafe key (it asks for it on first run):

  brew install rayoplateado/tap/jurl
  jurl -q "What is the Jevons paradox?" en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Stanley_Jevons
  jurl --code github.com/BurntSushi/ripgrep
  jurl -f "a cathedral" en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cologne
  jurl -l -n 3 news.ycombinator.com | xargs -n1 jurl -n 1
How it works: jurl splits the page into blocks, links and images, and turns each one into a yes/no question ("does this block answer the question?"). A decision model, Jev from TypeSafe, scores them all in a single request. For images, Clef on Cloudflare Workers AI looks at the pixels. The models return probabilities, never text: jurl picks, it doesn't write. Everything it prints is on the page, so it's safe to pipe into xargs curl.

Most pages take under a second and cost a fraction of a cent, about a thousand pages per dollar, paid straight to the APIs: jurl calls them directly with your own keys (TypeSafe for text, plus Cloudflare only if you want it to look at images).

Written in Rust, MIT or Apache-2.0. Code: https://github.com/rayoplateado/jurl

I'd especially like to hear about pages where it picks the wrong thing.

P.S. It's pronounced /xaɾl/, "harl": the name is a nod to the Spanish comedian Chiquito de la Calzada and his "jarl".

records.title: Show HN: MapLibre Compose, Interactive Vector Maps for Compose Multiplatform
records.author: sargunv
records.storyText:
MapLibre Compose is a Kotlin library for putting interactive vector maps in Compose Multiplatform apps on Android, iOS, desktop, and web. It's part of the MapLibre ecosystem, and isn't tied to any map provider; you point it at any MapLibre style and tile source: commercial, free, or your own.

- Docs: https://maplibre.org/maplibre-compose/

- Code: https://github.com/maplibre/maplibre-compose

- Live demo: https://maplibre.org/maplibre-compose/demo/

About two years ago, I started building a transit tracking app in Compose Multiplatform, and found there was no suitable map library for it with the level of customization I wanted. So, within my "train-tracking-app" repo, I started working on wrapping the MapLibre Android and iOS SDKs behind a common Compose API.

Around the same time, the StreetComplete folks and MapLibre Native folks were looking for the same thing: a Compose SDK for MapLibre Native. I spun my wrapper out into a library, and so began my two year yak shaving quest to bring MapLibre maps to Compose Multiplatform.

The SDK-wrapping approach got the first releases out quickly, but it didn't age well. I could only expose what both supported, and each had its own slightly different design and API contracts, as they were not designed to be used together. And there was no such sdk at all for desktop. I knew I needed to go a layer down, build on the MapLibre Native C++ core underpinning those Android and iOS SDKs. I first did this with JNI, on desktop only, with the help of GLM-4.5 to navigate some graphics work that I was deeply unfamiliar with. This worked, but JNI was tedious and bug-prone, AWT<>Compose interop was limited, and the work stalled. Around this time, I also onboarded the project into the MapLibre organization.

Earlier this year, I rebooted the native core wrapping effort. I designed a C API (https://github.com/maplibre/maplibre-native-ffi) wrapping the MapLibre Native C++ core, generated safe(ish) language bindings on top for KMP and many other languages (first with LLMs, now working on deterministic codegen), and rebuilt MapLibre Compose for desktop, Android, and iOS on that foundation. This cleared numerous blockers and bugs, and allowed me to bring the library to a feature-complete state.

This work shipped in the StreetComplete iOS public beta recently (https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49920160). Stadia's Ferrostar navigation SDK builds on it now too (https://stadiamaps.github.io/ferrostar/).

It's pre-1.0. Android, iOS, and desktop wrap MapLibre Native. Kotlin/JS still wraps MapLibre GL JS, and Kotlin/Wasm support is awaiting Compose v1.13. If you're interested in building map apps with Compose, I encourage you to try this out and share feedback as I'm working on refining the api surface before stabilization.

Now, two years later, I'm getting back to working on my transit tracking app, which I hope to share on HN in a couple months.

records.title: Show HN: Vibivibi – End-to-end encrypted sharing of Coding Agent sessions
records.author: hyluo
records.storyText:
Hi HN, I'm Hongyin. I built Vibivibi (https://vibivibi.com) because I kept starting a coding agent session on my laptop and wanting to continue it on a server, or hand it to a colleague. I want an easier way to do it but won’t trust anyone hosting my traces who promises they won’t sell it (market price per coding trace is $50 to $100).

What Vibivibi does: a small CLI, `vibi`, finds the sessions your coding agents keep locally (Claude Code, Codex CLI, OpenCode, Pi), encrypts one on your machine and uploads it. On another machine `vibi pull` puts it back where the agent expects it, so `claude --resume <id>` just continues. `vibi push` can also send a session to someone else by email.

Our service cannot read session content. Each user has a key pair made on their first machine; the private key reaches the server only wrapped with a key derived from an encryption password that never leaves the user's machines. Every session version is encrypted with its own random key, which is then wrapped for each recipient (X25519, HKDF, AES-256-GCM). The server sees account emails, public keys, machine names, sizes, timestamps, who sent what to whom, and an optional plain-text label.

Sending to someone who doesn't have an account yet works too: the sender's client makes a key pair on their behalf, locks it with a random 12-character passphrase, and shows the sender that passphrase to pass on out of band. When the recipient signs up and enrolls a machine, their client unlocks it locally and re-keys the session to their own key.

The client is open source (Apache-2.0): https://github.com/subconscious-systems/vibi-cli The crypto and the schemas of everything the client sends live in one package, so the claims above can be checked against the code. It ships as a single executable, no Node or npm needed: `curl -fsSL https://vibivibi.com/install.sh | sh`, or build it yourself. The server (Next.js on Vercel, Postgres, blob storage) is not open source.

Pricing: free for 200 MB of encrypted storage and unlimited sends; Pro is $8/month for 20 GB; Team is $15/seat with an admin view and a "send only inside the team" policy.

Honest limitations: - There is no password recovery. Forget the encryption password and the key, and everything encrypted for it, is gone.

I'd like to hear where the threat model falls short, and which agents or workflows you'd want supported next.

records.storyText:
I started Solarite several years ago because I wanted something simpler to use than the existing js ui frameworks. Features like:

- not having to setup a build environment or wait for compilation

- no signals or other dance to setup my data

- class based components, where I could pass arguments to sub-components as constructor args

records.title: Show HN: Orrery, a Three.js solar system visualization powered by real NAIF data
records.author: rybosome
records.storyText:
Hi HN, I'm excited to share a personal project that I've put a lot of love into.

This is Orrery[0], a Three.js-based visualization of our solar system. It allows the positions of the major bodies to be played and scrubbed through the years 1950 - 2050, with optional orbit path displays and various other visualization options.

The data comes from NAIF SPICE - a framework and set of open-source data kernels containing highly detailed space geometry data.

I was inspired to set out on this project when learning that NAIF SPICE, originally written in Fortran and C, lacks highly standardized JavaScript bindings. There are great Python (SpiceyPy) and Rust (Anise) bindings, among other languages, but nothing for JavaScript.

So, I developed tspice[1] to wrap the CSPICE library. It uses the Native API when running in Node, and an Emscripten binding around CSPICE when running in the browser. It uses a standardized backend abstraction that the runtime swaps in depending on which context its invoked with.

tspice offers an API that is meant to be a near-literal translation of the C APIs, along with higher-level functionality in separate namespaces. It also offers web conveniences like a dedicated web worker client (calculations can be intensive, you don't want them on your render thread) and caching.

tspice only wraps a subset of the CSPICE library, but it was enough that I wanted to build a simple visualization tool to test it. Eventually the visualization testbed became refined enough that it felt compelling on its own.

Although this is a hobby project, I'd love to hear suggestions and feedback on either Orrery or the underlying tspice library. If there are any folks in the planetary science community in particular who might be interested in tspice, please let me know if there are features that would make this more useful for you.

One feature I love is the ability to generate a share URL of a particular viewer state that you like. I'd really love to see any states that people find especially cool! One of my favorite views is this one[2].

Thanks for taking a look!

[0] Orrery repo: https://github.com/rybosome/orrery [1] tspice repo: https://github.com/rybosome/tspice [2] favorite orrery view: https://orrery.ryboso.me/dVPLbtswEPwX9qoIol4UdWtaB22RNEbsoii...

records.storyText: Evergreen Common Lisp implements tiered JIT compilation with on-stack replacement, and includes many other interesting features (fibers! JVM integration! static and dynamic linked binaries! tree-shaking! speculative optimization w/ deoptimization!) You can even run native Android apps on your phone and connect to them with sly (https://github.com/atgreen/evergreen-compose). It still has long way to go, and sometimes is comically bad, but the Android apps working is a milestone that is good enough to share v0.0.1. The Android apps build directly from asdf. You don't need any of the normal Android tooling, apart from adb (the debugger, to copy it to your phone and forward slynk ports). Made with AI, of course (>2k commits over 2 months).

records.title: Show HN: Reright.it – Human approval for agent-written text
records.author: paulofilip3
records.storyText:
So, I use agents to write a ton of stuff now: e-mails, client messages, commit messages, comments, etc.

The problem is that AI writing is VERY easy to spot and most of the time I don't want it being sent under my name, since it does not sound like me at all.

After failing at trying to fix it with rulebooks or skills like humanizer, I decided it was better to try to "catch" every time the agents write public-facing text and force the agents to send it to a single queue and wait for my editing and approval.

Why this approach?

I still want the agents to draft the text for me, since it's time consuming to pull up the necessary information and create the initial structure of the message.

All I need to make the text sound like me is to lightly re-structure some sentences, remove the enthusiasm, trim it down, remove words I don't use, etc..

So I made this for myself and have used it for a while now, find it very useful, so I decided to make it public.

If offers a nice looking UI with a proper text editor that allows me to easily edit and approve/reject public facing text produced by any of my running agents.

It's super simple, can be used locally or with cloud session agents (but hooks don't work there, so there's no way to enforce its use there).

Every message shows up as a draft that I can edit and it’s got all the context right there: what it is, who's gonna read it, and why the agent even wrote it.

Then, I can edit it, hit approve and the agent sends my version of the text.

I figured other people might also find it useful, so here it goes.

Any feedback is much appreciated.

records.title: Show HN: Productivity FOSS App Synced in Desktop and Mobile
records.author: philipthetenth
records.storyText:
Some of the many things it offers:

    - Plan: your week with time blocks, repeating or one-off. You can skip or move a single occurrence and save week templates. External calendars show next to it, and there’s an ICS feed out.
    - Board / Todos: today as a kanban board, plus undated todos with tags, filters, attributes and links. Putting a todo on a day schedules it.
    - Weekly review: clear out stale todos and write a note on the week.
    - Notebooks: notes per subject in folders, a diary, ideas, people (birthdays, relationships, every mention of them). Those work as scopes, they can hold everything mentioned here: goals, workouts, inventory, tasks, etc.
    - Goals: numeric targets and progress logs. You can link tasks to a goal, so finishing them moves it.
    - Health: habit tracking with a heatmap, and workouts that log reps, kg and km per exercise. You can put those on a date too, log how much weight you lifted, the distance you ran, etc.
    - Inventory / Shopping: things you own with quantities and restocking. Recipes use inventory items as ingredients, and what’s missing goes to the shopping list, which you can open offline in the market to see what is missing.
    - Finance: ledgers, statement import, auto-sorting rules, bills. Also integrates with inventory prices.
    - Media: a gallery and audio recordings. You can put those on notes and tasks, or standalone.
    - Reminders: on blocks and todos. You get notifications on the mobile app or PC.
A quick add (+) wheel menu for adding any important thing with one finger movement. Everything can have tags, many things can have attributes (key value pairs) that can be used with integrations: it comes with a REST API and a MCP server; you can use any AI to talk to it through scoped tokens that allow you to keep your privacy from AI companies by only giving it access to one particular project (Notebook) and its goals, tasks, notes, inventory items etc.

It’s keyboard-driven (vim-style keys) too, and you can run it in the phone both in sync with the official / you self-hosted instance, or fully isolated (never sees the internet).

records.title: Show HN: Carve – An open-source Mac agent with a choice of models
records.author: davidajackson
records.storyText:
Hi HN,

I built and open-sourced Carve to handle repetitive work in windows you already use.

Choose the window in any Mac app where you want it to work, press Option-D, and watch it do what you want. For example, in the demo I show an example CRM and Carve entering contact details and drafting a follow up. It also has the ability to annotate and explain items on the screen.

This runs with your own API keys, and can even support OpenRouter, though OpenAI is the best tested. Experimental adapters also for Bedrock, Azure. No reason it couldn't expand beyond experimental support to support more local models.

I built this because I found that Claude and Codex were rather clunky when using computer use, I like having a sleek window that just pops up and shows me what it's doing. Also it has the 3 similar modes (approve plan, step by step manual approval, or act directly mode).

Local currently covers browser actions via vision models, computer use support is required for operating other native mac apps. This is an ongoing area of work.

I'm seeing a lot of demand for local model support and building out relevant tooling so wanted to contribute. We're just now at the point where models are getting fast and smart enough to make rapid computer use possible. You can take a look at the benchmarks in the repository, Carve currently can rapidly and cheaply handle explaining, summarizing, basic navigation, and extraction. Complex, long horizon tasks are a work in progress, though I'm seeing promising results. Failures resemble patterns, and you can identify patterns and fix them by running evaluations in batches.

I'd love any feedback on how well the tool works, what you tried, and any issues that you found. Thank you!

records.title: Show HN: Twrctrl – Browser-Based Tower and Ground ATC Simulator
records.author: franklin0s
records.storyText:
I've been building this top-down browser-based air traffic control simulator where you handle the ground movement of aircraft after noticing that a vast majority of browser ATC simulators are focused on the radar/TRACON aspects of ATC that reduce our beautiful aircraft to dots on a screen with some text.

You handle everything between the runway and gates, issuing pushback, taxi, takeoff, and landing clearances to aircraft in this simulator, with aircraft logic and command mechanics working as close as I could to memory of how real ATC works. I've both flown planes as a student pilot and also hold aircraft maintenance certification so there is a lot of my judgement in this too.

These are all real airports, aircraft, weather, and operator patterns, referenced to publicly available airport data and satellite imagery, alongside input from fellow professionals in the industry.

There are synthetic aircraft engine sounds that use powerplant-specific sound parameters such as turbofans using N1%/N2% with turboprops having a TRQ% parameter in addition, tuned to match different general engine types. (like the howl of a CFM LEAP-1A/B being different to the buzzing of a RR RB211)

It works best on desktop, the phone mode is there but is a little bit clunky. No download or signup, all in the browser ready to go, with a quick tutorial under "how to play" to get you up to speed in aviation phraseology.

This is a quasi-simulator, based on real-world operations but with some game-like aspects to keep the player engaged and the overall simulator visually appealing. Keflavík (BIKF) and Stockholm-Arlanda (ESSA) are the two airports currently modelled in the simulator by yours truly.

I would love to hear anyone's thoughts, especially curious to get feedback on the mechanics and experience from ANSP-adjacent or aviation professionals.

records.title: Show HN: Browsentic Open-source Claude for Chrome alternative for any agent CLI
records.author: imshaikot
records.storyText:
A personal agent harness lives in your existing browser, connects to your claude-code (or any other major harness codex or cursor-cli...) NOT the SDK API, exposes web-optimized tools to the harness - that's Browsentic.

A free, opensource (Apache 2.0) with rich capabilities alternative to Comet, BrowserOS, Browser-use, Claude for Chrome or nanobrowser.

The unique architecture of Browsentic makes it different from all other alternatives. It uses a loopback MCP server that spawns claude/codex/OpenCode/Cursor harness in a detached process. You can already guess, it is a bi-directional MCP, you can browse agentic through the browser harness or through any MCP client.

Browsentic doesn't require any new browser to install and not limited to chromium, it supports Firefox as well. By default you don't even need CDP to perform core agentic browsing.

Capabilities: core accessibilities (50+ compare to nanobrowser only had 20), custom skill, record-replay, schedule-monitoring-notification, resolves captcha autonomously, has it's own memory, voice orb over web-speech API, can sideload custom tools, platform + browser + agent agnostic

It is opensource, no API key, no telemetry & local first and actively maintained and yesterday was the first public stable launch (v0.8.0)

Currently I'm the only author but every & any contribution or suggestion will be more than welcome :)

Source: https://github.com/imshaikot/browsentic

records.title: Show HN: The Velocity Trap, the Phoenix Project for the AI Age
records.author: ColinEberhardt
records.storyText:
I'm taking a bit of a risk with this one, this is a novella I authored with the help of AI. If that offends you, please move on!

Everyone on HN knows just how much AI is disrupting our industry. Although, much of the industry narrative focusses on the tools, the AI, the harnesses, and their ever-growing capabilities. We need to spend just as much, if not more time discussing the impact this is having on us. Humans will still be a significant part of the software engineering ‘system’, and many of us are rapidly trying to determine what our role will ultimately be.

Storytelling is a great medium for communicating and understanding change. That’s why I really enjoy books like The Phoenix Project — a vehicle for helping people understand the DevOps transformation from a human perspective.

This story is very much inspired by The Phoenix Project: a near-future account of the impact AI has on an organisation deep in the pursuit of speed, ignoring the risks and the human impact.

This story was written with the help of AI. While I can write a decent technical blog post, there is no hope for me when it comes to works of fiction! I have not tried to disguise the AI writing, and I have not suppressed the em dashes — although I did remove one use of the term “load-bearing”! If you consider an AI-authored tale to be worthless slop, I totally understand. I was simply using AI as a tool to help me tell a story that I think needs telling.

It helps reading social situations with multiple perspectives, and helps users rehearse hard conversations by simulating others with analyses and suggestions, there are also companions that knows the full context if users choose to share that can chat with them naturally. It can be both serious and entertaining, by switching different world views, and it fully respects users' privacy by keeping all texts encrypted.

In order to achieve modest performance, I built multi-regional gateway and a fine-tuned model integrating both quality and responding speed. The models are served on GPUs via Modal, with a second adapter just for the simulation, and reply latency went from 7.9s to about 2.0s.
